pr_title: detect-virt: check the inode number of the pid namespace
pr_body:
The indoe number of root pid namespace is hardcoded in the kernel to 0xEFFFFFFC since 3.8, so check the inode number of our pid namespace if all else fails. If it's not 0xEFFFFFFC then we are in a pid namespace, hence a container environment.

Fixes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/35249

As suggested by https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/35188#issuecomment-2489747807
pr_comments: It could be I got lost among all those PRs but as far as I understand https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/35256 was merged to make it easier to figure out what's going on. Has it ever been run in that environment? Is it possible to add a link to the results to the commit message?

IIUC, the first commit causes the following change in CentosCI jobs: previously TEST-74-AUXUTILS ran in a VM and in systemd-nspawn, and now it'll only run in a VM. @yuwata raised the point that reduces the coverage. So I think it's reasonable to drop that commit. There doesn't seem to be any strong justification for it.

> IIUC, the first commit causes the following change in CentosCI jobs: previously TEST-74-AUXUTILS ran in a VM and in systemd-nspawn, and now it'll only run in a VM. @yuwata raised the point that reduces the coverage. So I think it's reasonable to drop that commit. There doesn't seem to be any strong justification for it.

The bash stuff is either/or, not both. Running in a VM means more stuff is ran, not less, so more coverage. And it brings it in sync with mkosi runs, which is more important. We use mkosi to run tests these days, having tests running in wildly different environments depending on which runner is chosen seems very clearly a bug to me.

As already mentioned, if anybody wants to make TEST-74 runnable in nspawn, the tests requiring isolation can be moved out of it, and into somewhere else. And then both runners can remove the VM requirement.

> The bash stuff is either/or, not both. Running in a VM means more stuff is ran, not less, so more coverage.

No, that's not how the old runner works. A given test can be run in three different ways: in a VM, under nspawn, and under nspawn with user namespaces.

Making things consistent between the old and new runners would be reasonable, but since the former still gives more coverage, it's better not to do this at this point.

Please drop the first commit.

> > The bash stuff is either/or, not both. Running in a VM means more stuff is ran, not less, so more coverage.
> 
> No, that's not how the old runner works. A given test can be run in three different ways: in a VM, under nspawn, and under nspawn with user namespaces.

Exactly - and the first one gives the most coverage, given it enables more tests. The way the old script works is that it will not run a VM unless explicitly configured to do so, or it's impossible to do otherwise. Which means all the new tests that were added to TEST-74, including this one, are skipped, as it's not currently configured to run them.

> Making things consistent between the old and new runners would be reasonable, but since the former still gives more coverage, it's better not to do this at this point.

How is running _fewer_ tests giving _more_ coverage? Surely you meant the opposite?

Yu wrote:
> By default, centos cis run each test both in qemu and nspawn.

This is my understanding too. So without the setting, we run the test twice, in different environments.


> How is running _fewer_ tests giving _more_ coverage? Surely you meant the opposite?

Exactly, I mean the opposite.

> Yu wrote:
> 
> > By default, centos cis run each test both in qemu and nspawn.
> 
> This is my understanding too. So without the setting, we run the test twice, in different environments.

What do you mean by run twice? There's only one run as far as I can see? E.g. this is the log: https://jenkins-systemd.apps.ocp.cloud.ci.centos.org/job/upstream-vagrant-archlinux/19241/artifact/systemd-centos-ci/artifacts_uph7m0s_/vagrant-logs.mUU/vagrant-arch-testsuite.eXJ/TEST-74-AUX-UTILS_PASS.log

> > Yu wrote:
> > > By default, centos cis run each test both in qemu and nspawn.
> > 
> > 
> > This is my understanding too. So without the setting, we run the test twice, in different environments.
> 
> What do you mean by run twice? There's only one run as far as I can see? E.g. this is the log: https://jenkins-systemd.apps.ocp.cloud.ci.centos.org/job/upstream-vagrant-archlinux/19241/artifact/systemd-centos-ci/artifacts_uph7m0s_/vagrant-logs.mUU/vagrant-arch-testsuite.eXJ/TEST-74-AUX-UTILS_PASS.log

See https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/35273#discussion_r1852476361

> this is the log

This log shows this PR (where the test is skipped in nspawn) so it isn't surprising it's run in QEMU only I think.

https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/35273#discussion_r1852476361 points to the other log where it can be seen that it's run in qemu and nspawn. It should be possible to take a look at any other PR as well.

> IIUC, the first commit causes the following change in CentosCI jobs: previously TEST-74-AUXUTILS ran in a VM and in systemd-nspawn, and now it'll only run in a VM. @yuwata raised the point that reduces the coverage. So I think it's reasonable to drop that commit. There doesn't seem to be any strong justification for it.

To cut the story short, I've split the test up myself. Now TEST-74 doesn't have the VM config in either runners. Subtests (or part of subtests) that only run while under a VM are moved to a new TEST-87 which is configured to always run under a VM, with both runners. I hope this satisfies both you and @yuwata and we can make progress

Hm... I am not a fan of splitting the test into two. The justification/motivation of the first commit is based on misunderstanding of what CentOS CIs do currently. Did you read comments by @evverx above? It is completely not necessary to split the test into two. On CentOS CIs, test cases that can run both on qemu and nspawn (remaining in TEST-74 with the first commit) are actually run on both, and test cases that requires qemu (moved to TEST-87 by the first commit) are of course run on qemu. So, this does not change anything for CentOS CIs. This only changes how the test cases that can run on both qemu and nspawn are tested on mkosi based runner. 
- CentOS CIs (previous, and with this PR)

| test cases | qemu | nspawn |
| -- | :--: | :--: |
| can run on both | ✓ | ✓ |
| requires qemu | ✓ | ✗ |
- mkosi CI (previous)

| test cases | qemu | nspawn |
| -- | :--: | :--: |
| can run on both | ✓ | ✗ |
| requires qemu | ✓ | ✗ |
- mkosi CI (with this PR)

| test cases | qemu | nspawn |
| -- | :--: | :--: |
| can run on both | ✗ | ✓ |
| requires qemu | ✓ | ✗ |

So, at least, the commit message of the first commit is misleading. Still each CI does something different from each other. And, I do not find any improvement by the change. This just complicates the test scripts, and increases the cost of managing test cases.

BTW, the most discussion of this PR is completely irrelevant to the original issue. I'd like to merge #35291 at first, then continue to discuss about splitting or so here or at another later PR, as splitting test is not a release blocker.

> It is completely not necessary to split the test into two.

It is. It's just broken currently. Every single other test is either marked for VMs or not, it's just this one that is a weird mix-and-match, where depending on the runner something different happens. This is a bug and it needs to be fixed.

> BTW, the most discussion of this PR is completely irrelevant to the original issue. I'd like to merge https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/35291 at first, then continue to discuss about splitting or so here or at another later PR, as splitting test is not a release blocker.

No, let's not, this is ready to be merged, as whatever worry might have been about coverage, true or not, is resolved.

> It's just broken currently. Every single other test is either marked for VMs or not, it's just this one that is a weird mix-and-match, where depending on the runner something different happens.

No, you misunderstand what CentOS CIs do. Please read the above comments by @evverx and @keszybz (and mine...).
And, the 'weird mix-and-match' is not a problem. The integration tests (not only TEST-74) are intentionally designed so.

> And, the 'weird mix-and-match' is not a problem. The integration tests (not only TEST-74) are intentionally designed so.

Yes, this is a problem, because if you run `sudo make` on your machine and I run `meson test` on mine, we will get two different things. This is a bug. These are not designed for that at all, in fact the legacy bash stuff is not really designed in the first place, it just happened.

> > And, the 'weird mix-and-match' is not a problem. The integration tests (not only TEST-74) are intentionally designed so.
> 
> Yes, this is a problem, because if you run `sudo make` on your machine and I run `meson test` on mine, we will get two different things. This is a bug. These are not designed for that at all, in fact the legacy bash stuff is not really designed in the first place, it just happened.

I disagree. All integration tests were originally designed to run both under QEMU _and_ nspawn, since as was already mentioned the tools might behave differently in these two environments. Some tests were explicitly skipped in either if they didn't make sense to run there (like udev or initrd tests in nspawn containers). This was later tweaked a bit by introducing `TEST_PREFER_NSPAWN=` and friends to accommodate for slower/busy CIs, but that was a compromise between speed and coverage. CentOS CI, for the most part, tried to push for the latter (which means running tests under both QEMU _and_ nspawn), since it had resources to do so.

But that's just my 5 cents. I haven't had much time to follow the mkosi stuff for the past several months, so maybe things changed, this merely describes how things used to be.

hmm, i don't grok why the test organization has to be changed like this. Why not just change the added line to the test to:

```sh
# If we have the privs to, create a quick pidns container and verify we detect this properly
if ! systemd-detect-virt --container ; then
        unshare --mount-proc --fork --user --pid systemd-detect-virt --container
fi
```

seems to be much simpler.

in general i think we should run as much of the testuite on all environments, and only exclude the minimal tests we really have to. I mean, stuff such as testing udev makes zero sense in a container, so we can exclude that fully, but otherwise I really don't see why the systemd-detect-virt stuff should not be run inside both nspawn and vm

> > > And, the 'weird mix-and-match' is not a problem. The integration tests (not only TEST-74) are intentionally designed so.
> > 
> > 
> > Yes, this is a problem, because if you run `sudo make` on your machine and I run `meson test` on mine, we will get two different things. This is a bug. These are not designed for that at all, in fact the legacy bash stuff is not really designed in the first place, it just happened.
> 
> I disagree. All integration tests were originally designed to run both under QEMU _and_ nspawn, since as was already mentioned the tools might behave differently in these two environments. Some tests were explicitly skipped in either if they didn't make sense to run there (like udev or initrd tests in nspawn containers). This was later tweaked a bit by introducing `TEST_PREFER_NSPAWN=` and friends to accommodate for slower/busy CIs, but that was a compromise between speed and coverage. CentOS CI, for the most part, tried to push for the latter (which means running tests under both QEMU _and_ nspawn), since it had resources to do so.

That's not what I meant. We have the TEST_NO_NSPAWN variable (and it's opposite, TEST_NO_QEMU) to mark test cases that can only run in one but not the other, to clearly separate them. And we've always used it, so that the functionality that needs VM (or container) can be separated into their own tests, so that you know that they are either fully running, or they are fully skipped: cryptsetup, udev, etc. It's problematic to have half-and-half in the upstream CI, as without checking the individual journal log for each test case, you can't really know if the test really passed, or if it was just skipped, which is a needless additional burden. And this is a problem in the upstream CI, where we want full coverage, as much as possible.

TEST-74 was always a container-friendly one, a 'catch-all' for quick smoke tests for auxiliary utilities that didn't have a place elsewhere, and only very recently gained a few subtests that are VM only. There is no law of physic or design or anything else that says it has to be so, and in fact it's much better if it isn't.

> in general i think we should run as much of the testuite on all environments, and only exclude the minimal tests we really have to. I mean, stuff such as testing udev makes zero sense in a container, so we can exclude that fully, but otherwise I really don't see why the systemd-detect-virt stuff should not be run inside both nspawn and vm

systemd-detect-virt is ran in both. The test case that doesn't make sense in the nspawn test is moved to the vm test, the test case that makes sense in nspawn is in nspawn, and the test case that works in both, is in both. This is how this was always organized: things that can run in both are in tests that can run in both, and things that can only run in VM are in tests explicitly marked as such, like udev, cryptsetup, portabled, and so on. Just check all the TEST_NO_NSPAWN definitions under the test/*/test.sh files.

> TEST-74 was always a container-friendly one, a 'catch-all' for quick smoke tests for auxiliary utilities that didn't have a place elsewhere, and only very recently gained a few subtests that are VM only. There is no law of physic or design or anything else that says it has to be so, and in fact it's much better if it isn't.

Also test-74 is a catch-all that does a lot, and will get more and more. Having it run in a VM in mkosi makes it slower unnecessarily. VM-only tests should be scoped to the minimum they need to do, to reduce runtime. By refactoring the VM-only part away, it can run again in a container in mkosi.

> > TEST-74 was always a container-friendly one, a 'catch-all' for quick smoke tests for auxiliary utilities that didn't have a place elsewhere, and only very recently gained a few subtests that are VM only. There is no law of physic or design or anything else that says it has to be so, and in fact it's much better if it isn't.
> 
> Also test-74 is a catch-all that does a lot, and will get more and more. Having it run in a VM in mkosi makes it slower unnecessarily. VM-only tests should be scoped to the minimum they need to do, to reduce runtime. By refactoring the VM-only part away, it can run again in a container in mkosi.

I want to change the mkosi runner to not fix the environment anymore actually. The environment that is used should be user controlled so we can run tests in either nspawn, qemu or vmspawn (or anything else we add later). So to me it makes sense that individual tests skip themselves based on the environment they're run in.

I think the current grouping of tests is very arbitrary and we'll need to come up with something more comprehensive to allow properly distributing tests across multiple containers/VMs without running each test in a separate container/VM.

But this really needs more comprehensive changes to the testsuite again, this change, while of course a quick fix, doesn't really address the core issue, so given the amount of discussion this generates which is just a pointless waste of time, I wouldn't bother trying to get this in and instead we should discuss a more comprehensive rework of the test grouping and how we handle different environments.

All of these changes will also become much easier once we can get rid of the bash runner and replace it with mkosi, but this also requires extra work on the mkosi runner to handle coredumps, coverage, valgrind and all the other things CentOS CI does now.

So given there's tons of non-controversial work to be done on the integration test suite, I implore everyone to stop wasting time discussing one controversial change like this and instead focus on the non-controversial stuff that everyone agrees on.

I completely agree. Though systemd has never been tested with Valgrind upstream so it certainly shouldn't be a blocker in terms of removing the bash runner and switching to the mkosi testing infrastructure anywhere.
The second patch was merged via #35306. And the split is very controversial. Let's close this.

> I want to change the mkosi runner to not fix the environment anymore actually. The environment that is used should be user controlled so we can run tests in either nspawn, qemu or vmspawn (or anything else we add later). So to me it makes sense that individual tests skip themselves based on the environment they're run in.

It's fine that tests skip themselves, but it needs to be at the test level, not subtest. Otherwise it becomes very opaque what the result of a CI run actually is, which is extremely important for the upstream CI jobs, where we want clarity at the glance of an eye. If I get 80/80 pass, but I need to go and look into the journal of each test (which we don't save anyway on success, so can't even do that) to actually figure out if that test run covered everything or not, that is extremely sub-optimal and error-prone. Nobody is going to do that.
That's why it makes more sense to use the approach we use for all the other tests: the full test needs a VM to run, and is skipped (and marked as such) if that can't be done. Then you get 40/80 pass and 40 skips, and it's clear what the degree of coverage of that run is. Agan this is extremely important for the upstream CI, as we want maximum coverage, and maximum clarity.

> I think the current grouping of tests is very arbitrary and we'll need to come up with something more comprehensive to allow properly distributing tests across multiple containers/VMs without running each test in a separate container/VM.

And that's fine to do later, but it doesn't need to block fixing the one odd case that is currently around. For example right now in packit since I've switched it to mkosi, we lose coverage of TEST-74, just because a handful of subtests can't run in nspawn. That is not ideal.

> And the split is very controversial. Let's close this.

Sorry but this makes no sense. We rearrange these tests all the time. Why should something like it ever be controversial? It's running the same things, in a different setup, that provides greater clarity. I'll reopen this without the other change.

> we want maximum coverage, and maximum clarity

I don't think it makes much sense to discuss coverage with no actual coverage reports anywhere in sight. "40 skips" is a meaningless metric given that 1 skip can mean significant coverage drops. I think it would be nice to move this discussion to https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/34271 (or open a new issue where it can be discussed publicly)
